kurz: Consulting Deep Dive, part 4: Bain, the firm that turned private equity into its calling card
Strasbourg bars a lawyer for two years over AI-invented case law, a first for the human rights court
Canva adds an AI off switch, just as AI assistants start eating its lunch

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 4: Bain, the firm that turned private equity into its calling card
meldungen.text:
Of the three MBB firms, Bain is the one most closely associated with private equity, and the reputation is earned. Its Private Equity Group (PEG) is a global practice of more than 1,000 professionals that, in Bain's own description, accompanies investors through the entire life of a deal: generating ideas for targets, running due diligence, and planning the eventual exit. The bread and butter is commercial due diligence (CDD): in a matter of weeks, a small team establishes whether a target's market, competitive position and growth plan justify the price a fund is about to pay. Bain's job postings for PEG associates describe them leading diligence workstreams in sectors such as technology, retail and healthcare, often juggling one to three live cases at once. The pace is relentless, but the reps are exactly what investors later look for.

Crucially, PE work is not confined to specialists. Bain says every consultant who joins can work in the private equity practice and is encouraged simply to tell their recruiting contact that they are interested. Interview guides note that Bain's case interviews frequently take the form of a due diligence question ("should our client buy this company?"), and that sector knowledge helps but is not required. In a Bain podcast, partner Rebecca Burack argues that consultants should seek out PE cases early in their careers, because some colleagues who avoided them later regretted it.

The ladder is compact. You start as Associate Consultant (the usual entry after a bachelor's or master's degree), then become Consultant, Manager (formerly called Case Team Leader), Associate Partner (formerly Principal), Partner and Senior Partner. Strong performers can be promoted six months to a year ahead of the standard pace, according to career guides.

The private equity link runs deep in Bain's history. Bain Capital was founded in 1984 by former Bain & Company partners, among them Mitt Romney, who later returned to steady the consultancy as interim chief executive in the early 1990s before going into politics. Many Bain Capital staff began their careers at Bain & Company. Career guides consistently describe Bain as the MBB firm with the strongest pipeline into private equity, with typical moves after two to four years, although the switch remains fiercely competitive and only a minority make it. Other well-trodden paths lead into operating roles and the corner office: Meg Whitman, who went on to run eBay, and Kenneth Chenault, later chief executive of American Express, both passed through Bain. One career guide estimates that around 10 per cent of MBB consultants leave for start-ups, as founders or early hires, though that figure is an estimate rather than official data.

The setting for all this is a PE industry in flux. Bain's own Global Private Equity Report 2026 describes a "K-shaped recovery" in which a small set of elite funds thrives while most struggle, and fee concessions to investors have steadily eroded managers' revenue. For a Bain consultant, that means diligence demand is concentrated among the strongest funds, which are also the most selective hirers. Bain does not publish which schools feed its DACH offices; that question, including your set of HEC, HSG, INSEAD, LBS, WHU and Nova, will be covered in part 16 of this series.

meldungen.titel: Oliver Wyman buys Synpulse, adding 1,200 financial services technologists to its strategy bench
meldungen.text:
Oliver Wyman, the management consulting arm of the insurance broker and advisory group Marsh, announced on Thursday that it has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a technology consultancy and AI platform company that works for banks, insurers, wealth managers and other financial institutions. Terms were not disclosed. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to the usual conditions and regulatory approvals.

Synpulse, founded in 1996 and based in Switzerland, employs around 1,200 people at more than 20 locations, who will keep working from offices in North America, Europe and Asia. Its business spans strategy, design, technology implementation and operations, with a dedicated technology division, Synpulse8, and a network of more than 100 ecosystem partners. Its speciality is the unglamorous core of financial services transformation: modernising legacy systems, streamlining operations and getting new products to market faster. The two firms have already staffed several end-to-end transformations with joint teams.

The logic is one the whole industry is chasing. "Our clients don't separate strategy from technology and execution," said Ted Moynihan, chief executive of Oliver Wyman and Marsh Management Consulting. Synpulse's co-chief executives, Konrad Niggli and Yves Roesti, said the combination would let them take on larger and more complex projects and invest more heavily in AI. It is the latest in a string of bolt-ons for Oliver Wyman, which agreed to buy the Dallas turnaround specialist CR3 Partners in May; Marsh, with annual revenue of 27 billion dollars and more than 95,000 staff, is also pursuing the investment firm Wilshire.

meldungen.titel: The Alvarez & Marsal Excel test: what candidates for restructuring and valuation roles should expect
meldungen.text:
Alvarez & Marsal (A&M), the restructuring and turnaround specialist that features later in this series, runs a recruitment process with an extra hurdle that general strategy consultancies tend to skip: a practical Excel or accounting test. Management Consulted has just published a guide to it, and candidate accounts on PrepLounge and Wall Street Oasis fill in the detail.

According to an overview of A&M's six-stage process, the skills test comes after the recruiter screen and applies mainly to restructuring, transaction advisory and valuation roles. The format varies by office and practice. One candidate describes being handed operational data from a plant and given about 30 minutes for a "quick and dirty" analysis, analytical rather than a full model. Others report a restructuring assessment built around a pivot table and the interpretation of a discounted cash flow valuation, sometimes with short written answers. Some offices replace the Excel exercise with numerical and verbal reasoning tests.

For associate roles in the private equity performance improvement practice, forum advice is that assessors care above all about clean structure and logic: linking operational assumptions through to EBITDA and cash flow, rather than building elaborate models. The recommended preparation is unglamorous but effective: fluency with pivot tables, lookup and conditional formulas (VLOOKUP, SUMIF and the like), keyboard shortcuts, quick cash-flow analyses, and sharp mental arithmetic, since time pressure is part of the test. Online assessments should be completed promptly, as later interview slots are filled on a rolling basis.

meldungen.titel: Strasbourg bars a lawyer for two years over AI-invented case law, a first for the human rights court
meldungen.text:
The European Court of Human Rights has, for the first time, sanctioned a lawyer for AI hallucinations. A Romanian advocate may not represent clients before the Strasbourg court for two years after filing a brief, drafted with an AI tool, that cited fictitious precedents, quoted paragraphs that never appeared in genuine judgments and invoked rulings that had nothing to do with the case or even contradicted her own argument.

She conceded "inaccuracies" and "citation errors"; the chamber called that an understatement, finding that some of the cited judgments had simply not been checked at all, when even a cursory search of the court's own database would have exposed them as fabrications. The judges were also irked at the time lost: verifying the claims and pursuing the disciplinary procedure, they said, had impaired the administration of justice. The court's president confirmed the exclusion on 13 November. Readmission is possible later, and the clients remain represented by a second lawyer on the case.

Under the same procedural rule, 44D, the court has excluded 25 lawyers over the past decade, but never before for AI fabrications. Internally it confines AI to administrative tasks and is drafting guidelines for parties and counsel, due shortly.

meldungen.titel: An autonomous AI hacking tool is blamed for knocking out the European Commission's staff systems for days
meldungen.text:
A Commission spokesman confirmed on Thursday that an AI-generated cyber campaign had hit the institution. It was detected on 22 October and confirmed four days later; several applications were taken offline as a precaution, notably Sysper, the HR platform for payslips, leave and time recording, and MyPMO, used to reimburse medical costs. Both were restored early this week, though Sysper crashed briefly again on Wednesday, and internal translation services failed on Tuesday. Salaries were paid, but many staff could neither log hours nor request leave. According to the Commission, no personal data appear to have been stolen; an anonymous official had initially told Politico that extensive personal data might have been compromised. Investigations continue.

The suspected weapon is Artex, an LLM-driven autonomous penetration-testing platform first published as open source, against which CERT-EU had already warned publicly in early November. An FBI alert says attackers have abused the Go framework since at least August to automate whole attack chains, from reconnaissance through exploiting misconfigurations to exfiltration, in some cases reaching privileged access in under three hours. It turns plain-language objectives into commands for specialised agents, calling external models such as Claude, GPT or DeepSeek; attackers favour the Chinese models, the FBI says, because they are cheap and show no recognisable safeguards.

The original developer, "Autumn-27", pulled the project from GitHub in October, but copies and a commercial variant still circulate; researchers counted more than 1,600 publicly reachable instances in early November.

meldungen.titel: Gemini 4 Neon: Google claims third place in the AI rankings, and first in coding, at a discount
meldungen.text:
Google DeepMind on Wednesday released Gemini 4 Neon, the fourth member of its Gemini 4 family in roughly seven weeks. Neon is pitched as the middle tier between Hydrogen, the fast everyday model that now powers Google Search, and Carbon, the slow and expensive flagship for the hardest long-running tasks. It replaces Argon, which had been reserved for cybersecurity defenders, and Gemini 3.1 Pro is being retired. In the Gemini app the three now appear as "Everyday help", "Deeper analysis" and the tier for the most complex work.

On the independent Intelligence Index from Artificial Analysis, Neon scores 61 points at its highest reasoning setting, enough for third place behind OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2. Its stronger suit is coding: on the Coding Agent Index it takes first place with 59 points, a whisker ahead of Claude Code running Fable 5.2 or Opus 5.5 (58 each), and an average task costs 6.86 dollars, against 12.61 for Opus 5.5 and 15.47 for Fable 5.2. On a benchmark for office work it also leads for presentation quality, 45 Elo points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Pricing is 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output tokens, with 95 per cent off cached input; Hydrogen costs exactly half. The headline claim of "Carbon performance at half the price" deserves scrutiny, however: it rests on Carbon's regular rate, which only applies from December, when Carbon doubles from its introductory 2 and 10 dollars. Until then Carbon is cheaper per token, and Neon uses about 15 per cent more output tokens per task. Many of Google's other top scores have yet to be independently confirmed, and with four models in seven weeks, choosing the right one is becoming a chore in itself.

meldungen.titel: Anthropic prices its listing at 83 dollars a share, well above the range, and starts trading on Nasdaq today
meldungen.text:
Anthropic has set the final price for its initial public offering at 83 dollars per share, comfortably above the originally indicated range of 70 to 78 dollars. Even on Tuesday evening, the talk had been of 80 dollars or more. The shares are due to begin trading on Nasdaq today; regular US trading opens at 15:30 Central European time, although with offerings of this size the first trade can come some time into the session. A debut above the issue price is widely expected.

Demand was extraordinary. According to CNBC, institutional orders reached roughly 400 billion dollars by the close of the book on Tuesday evening, and anonymous sources put retail demand at close to 100 billion dollars, implying the deal was at least six times oversubscribed. Many who put in orders will receive nothing. Anthropic raised the number of shares on offer from the roughly 801 million in its prospectus to more than 956 million, bringing gross proceeds to 79.4 billion dollars. If the underwriting banks exercise their greenshoe option on a further 147 million shares within 30 days, another 12.2 billion dollars would follow, and some existing shareholders are also selling just under 24 million shares at the outset. German-language media are already calling it the largest flotation in history, eclipsing the record held by SpaceX.

One detail has caused confusion in Europe: the European prospectus quotes a price of 120 dollars. That figure is a regulatory placeholder; the final price in the EU and Switzerland is identical to the US offer price.

Not everyone is celebrating. Activists plan to protest in Times Square as trading starts, warning that the listing puts pension money at risk, and sceptics question whether circular financing flows and multibillion-dollar computing commitments justify a valuation of up to 1.4 trillion dollars. This week six US state treasurers also demanded more disclosure on how Anthropic manages AI risk and why shareholders have so little say.

Update 08:50: Anthropic's own release puts the final offering at 980 million Class A shares (up from 825 million), of which about 956 million are new and 23.6 million come from the seven co-founders, who each sell around 3.4 million shares for roughly 280 million dollars and keep about 240 million apiece. Including a concurrent 26 billion dollar private placement with Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC at the same price, the company takes in more than 105 billion dollars. At about 81.3 billion dollars in total proceeds this is now confirmed as the largest IPO ever, ahead of SpaceX's 75 billion in June. On a fully diluted basis Anthropic is worth around 1.5 trillion dollars (eleventh among listed companies, just ahead of Tesla); counting only shares outstanding, about 1.1 trillion, or roughly 25 times its annualised revenue of 33.2 billion dollars, against some 49 times for SpaceX at its debut. The ticker is "ANT". For perspective: the FTX bankruptcy estate sold about 445 million shares in 2024 for 1.34 billion dollars; they would now be worth about 37 billion.

Update 17:55: Demand at the open was ferocious. Nasdaq's indicated price climbed to 110 dollars (about 99 euros), roughly 33 per cent above the 83 dollar offer, after earlier indications of 105; at that level Anthropic would be worth about 2 trillion dollars fully diluted, or some 1.5 trillion on shares outstanding, which Der Standard notes is twice Austria's GDP. Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell, the chief executive vowing that the company "will not bend to either business or political pressure". The pop would comfortably beat SpaceX, which opened 11 per cent up in June, closed its first day 19 per cent higher, peaked at 225 dollars and now trades around 145. Anthropic is floating more than 7 per cent of its shares against SpaceX's 4, and up to 316 million insider shares may be sold from day one, while most holders are locked up for 180 days and the co-founders for up to a year. The capital is needed: Anthropic has committed to more than 900 billion dollars in computing deals.

meldungen.titel: Nvidia quietly stops shipping H200 chips to China, abandoning the market its former chief fought for
meldungen.text:
Nvidia has stopped delivering its advanced H200 AI processors to China, even though the White House approved such sales last December. Interim chief executive Colette Kress disclosed the change almost in passing during Tuesday's earnings call: the company's guidance includes no licensed Hopper data centre products, and Nvidia is "no longer shipping" them to China. She gave no reason and did not say whether Nvidia would pursue other business there.

The reversal is striking because Jensen Huang, who stepped down as chief executive last week after reports of several extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman US intelligence suspected of being a Chinese spy, had lobbied hard for the right to sell the chips in China. Yet the business was troubled well before the scandal. Questions had been raised about whether the Chinese companies cleared to handle the H200 were properly vetted, and Reuters reported this month that around 600,000 of the chips were stuck in Hong Kong because Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports as it seeks to reduce its dependence on American technology.

The upshot is that the world's most valuable chipmaker is now, in effect, writing off China for its high-end data centre products, at least for the time being, while Beijing pushes its own suppliers. For investors, the strong quarter reported on Tuesday therefore comes without the Chinese upside that analysts had once pencilled in.

meldungen.titel: Microsoft Ignite: Azure becomes a platform for AI agents, and Windows moves further into the cloud
meldungen.text:
At its annual Ignite conference, Microsoft set out how it wants Azure to become the central platform for building and running AI agents. It is merging its Foundry AI service more closely with the Azure Kubernetes Service, creating one infrastructure for operating, securing and managing AI applications both in the cloud and on premises. Microsoft stresses open-source tools such as Kubernetes, vLLM and Ray, which also cover GPU environments outside Azure, so customers can choose models and environments freely. New features include Agent Sandbox, which isolates agents at virtual machine level, and Agent Grid for secure communication between agents, models and services. A new resource manager spreads load across GPU capacity and caches frequently used context so it need not be recomputed, and agents can now not only query but also create resources via the MCP protocol.

Security gets its own team of agents under the name Perception: a red team simulates attacks, a blue team triages alerts and investigates incidents, and a green team fixes vulnerabilities, with human experts setting the rules and monitoring costs on a dashboard. A tool called Azure Catalyst, combining Azure Migrate and GitHub Copilot Modernization, promises AI-driven renovation of legacy software, including a "Value Uplift" function that weighs modernisation costs against expected benefits. Microsoft says customers have already modernised 1.4 million applications this way; GitHub itself ported the Copilot runtime from TypeScript to Rust, producing more than 800,000 lines of production code.

Windows is to be developed into a secure operating system for agents, with "Hybrid Intelligence" letting models run either on the device or in Azure. Cloud PCs with GPU support are due in preview early next year, and Windows Server 2028 is available as a public preview, tuned for AI inference alongside business applications. Microsoft also introduced seven new models, among them MAI Cyber 2 Flash, which it claims beats OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on a cybersecurity benchmark at under 2 per cent of the cost per task, and a low-cost model called Microsoft-Decision-1.1. Some Azure virtual machines now run on the Cobalt 200 processor, said to be up to 50 per cent faster than its predecessor.

meldungen.titel: Canva adds an AI off switch, just as AI assistants start eating its lunch
meldungen.text:
Canva, the Australian design platform, has given every user a way to banish generative AI from its interface. A new toggle, "Enable generative AI features", found under Profile, Settings, Permissions, switches off tools such as Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Magic Expand, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes and image generation in the Canva chatbot. A second option, under Your account, AI personalisation, pushes human-made templates and graphics to the top of library searches, although it does not hide AI content entirely. Both settings are available to free and Pro accounts; until now only administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams and Education plans could restrict AI for their staff.

The switch is not a clean break. Background Remover and Magic Grab stay on, because, Canva argues, they merely rework existing images rather than generate anything new. Nor is the company retreating: the future of creativity "isn't a choice between AI and no AI," it says. Usage of its AI features has roughly doubled since a relaunch in September, and it recently unveiled its own models, Craft and Brush, to bring compute costs down.

The timing, however, is awkward. Canva is in the midst of the first company-wide restructuring in its history, cutting 1,271 roles, or 22 per cent of its workforce. It now expects revenue growth of about 20 per cent this year instead of the planned 30 (after 38 per cent last year); its largest backer, Blackbird, has marked its valuation down to 34.9 billion dollars, and the flotation pencilled in for 2027 has reportedly been shelved. The cuts reach Vienna, too: Canva Austria, built on the remove.bg start-up Kaleido acquired in 2021, has around 80 staff and earned 14.9 million euros after tax in 2025, but Canva will not say how many are affected.

The deeper threat comes from chat windows. Social media graphics, presentations, logos and photo edits that once needed a Canva template now take a single prompt in ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, and Anthropic is attacking the market head-on with Claude Design. Figma's shares are down about 44 per cent this year, and vibe-coding tools such as Lovable build entire sites from a sentence. Canva still has more than 250 million monthly users and a decade of profitability behind it, and users who arrive via AI assistants are almost twice as likely to pay.

meldungen.titel: Can Claude replace Office? heise tests how far Anthropic's built-in tools already go
meldungen.text:
heise online has examined how far Claude can now stand in for a conventional office suite, and the answer is: further than a year ago, but not all the way. Anthropic has steadily added its own productivity tools to the chat. Claude Docs, launched in September as a beta, lets you create and edit documents directly in a conversation and is now available on all plans, with export to Word, PDF and Markdown. Claude Slides, initially reserved for Pro and Max subscribers, produces presentations that can be exported to PowerPoint. Sheets and Whiteboards are in beta for paying users, Claude Dashboards has been renamed Claude Data and is generally available, and Claude Meetings has started as a beta.

The limits are clearest with spreadsheets. According to the heise report, Anthropic's own product manager concedes that Sheets is still simple and that established spreadsheet programs keep the upper hand for complex financial models; for those, Anthropic itself points to Excel and partner tools. Rather than trying to displace Microsoft outright, Anthropic also offers an Excel add-in and a Word integration that sit inside Office. Commentators add a sensible caveat: final documents for clients should not leave the building without a human check.

The picture changes quickly, since the beta tools are being extended almost weekly, but the direction is plain: for drafting, summarising and structuring, Claude is becoming a workplace in its own right, while heavy number crunching stays in dedicated software.

meldungen.titel: Europe's start-up lobby asks Brussels to scrap its own EU Inc proposal rather than accept a watered-down version
meldungen.text:
The most ardent champions of the EU Inc, the planned pan-European company form for start-ups, are pulling the emergency brake. Startups for Europe, the Brussels umbrella body of national start-up associations, and the EU-INC initiative led by the Austrian investor Andreas Klinger, which counts more than 26,000 supporters, have asked Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to withdraw the proposal and table it afresh. AustrianStartups, a founding member whose chief executive Hannah Wundsam sits on the umbrella group's board, backs the move. Days earlier, Ann Mettler of the European Innovation Council board and three law professors had called for the same.

The reason is the common position the member states agreed in the Council in October. "The Commission's proposal from March isn't everything we fought for, but it works," says Wundsam. According to the start-up groups, the Council text guts its core: banks, registries and authorities may treat an EU Inc differently, and a host country can challenge its registered office on "serious doubts"; companies with 750 or more employees or 150 million euros in revenue can no longer grant new staff equity under the European scheme, and the guarantee of no less favourable tax treatment has gone; incorporation by digital power of attorney and the central EU register have been struck out, with digital procedures pushed back to July 2028 at the earliest; and the simple digital wind-down procedure has been replaced by national insolvency law.

A legal analysis by EU-INC counts 16 points that would have to be restored, 12 of them essential, far more than trilogue talks between Parliament, Council and Commission usually settle. The likely outcome, they argue, is a company form nobody would use. "In its current form, European start-ups will keep incorporating in Delaware," says Wundsam, who also points the finger at national capitals, Vienna included, and plans fresh talks with Parliament and the Austrian government.

Not everyone wants to start over. Germany's Startup Association called the Council deal "an important step", welcomes that notary-free share transfers survived, and pins its hopes on the trilogue, while criticising the equity cap for penalising precisely the scale-ups that need it. The Irish Council presidency hailed the agreement; the European Trade Union Confederation, from the opposite side, wants the process halted over workers' rights. Parliament's legal affairs committee has repeatedly failed to agree its position on worker participation, so the trilogue cannot even begin, and a withdrawal would send the whole file back to square one.

meldungen.titel: Deutsche Telekom puts 100 million euros into Mistral, betting on a French model for "sovereign" AI in German industry
meldungen.text:
Deutsche Telekom has bought into Mistral AI. T.Capital Tech Fund, the group's strategic investment arm, which manages more than 2 billion euros, has invested 100 million euros in the Paris company's Series D. Telekom presents the stake as the first step towards a strategic partnership to bring trusted European AI to German businesses and public institutions, with industry and regulated sectors as the priority.

The division of labour is straightforward: Telekom supplies its sovereign infrastructure (notably its Industrial AI Cloud in Germany), customer relationships and integration know-how; Mistral contributes its frontier models, enterprise software and deployment expertise, building on its recently opened hub in Munich. Ferri Abolhassan, Telekom board member and chief executive of T-Systems, argued that businesses must be able to trust the technology while keeping control of their data; Mistral's finance chief Johan Bergqvist called Germany "the industrial backbone of Europe".

Telekom is joining an already enormous round. Mistral announced the Series D in September at 3 billion euros, the largest equity round ever raised by a European tech company, led by Samsung Electronics with PSG Equity and the European Commission's Scaleup Europe Fund (managed by EQT) as co-leads. Mistral is also buying growth: it acquired Emmi AI from Linz at a reported valuation of up to 330 million euros, and Linz is now an official Mistral location. Technologically, though, there is ground to make up, since its flagship Mistral Large 4 still trails the best open models from China.

The contest for Germany's sovereign AI market is getting crowded. SAP plans to serve the public sector with OpenAI via its subsidiary Delos Cloud, and the Schwarz Group is building its own sovereign cloud with Stackit and Schwarz Digits. The backdrop is sobering: according to the latest State of European Tech report, the United States invested five times as much in AI in nine months as Europe did in a decade.

meldungen.titel: First Circle Capital: an Austrian co-founder closes a 26 million dollar fund for Africa's "FinTech 2.0"
meldungen.text:
First Circle Capital, a pan-African venture firm co-founded by the Austrian-born investor Agnes Aistleitner, has held the final close of its First Circle Africa Fund I at 26 million dollars (about 23.3 million euros). The fund backs fintech start-ups at pre-seed and seed stage. Aistleitner founded the firm in 2021 with Selma Ribica, a former executive at the Kenyan mobile-payments pioneer M-Pesa, and Robert Smith, a former strategy consultant with East African experience. The women-led team has offices in Kampala, Nairobi, Casablanca and Cape Town.

The money comes mainly from development finance: IFC (the World Bank's private-sector arm, committing up to 6 million dollars, partly from a programme for women entrepreneurs), Bpifrance, the Dutch Good Growth Fund, FSD Africa, Egypt's MSMEDA, the Stellar Foundation and the Madagascan conglomerate Axian. The thesis, "FinTech 2.0", holds that the first wave of African fintech solved payments and mobile money, and that the next must close the remaining gaps: insurance, alternative lending, interoperability and financial infrastructure, climate fintech, fintech software and regtech. So far the firm has backed 18 start-ups, among them TurnStay (cross-border payments for travel bookings), WafR (digital payments in Moroccan corner shops) and Orca Fraud (AI-based fraud detection); several are said to be approaching Series A.

Aistleitner, who splits her time between Nairobi and Kampala, previously spent more than a decade building textile manufacturing businesses in Jordan and Ukraine and a tech company in Uganda. She describes venture capital as a business of probability distributions in which, in Africa above all, relationships and trust decide.

The timing is hardly easy. African start-ups raised about 2.4 billion dollars from January to October, 12 per cent less than a year earlier, and October alone fell 58 per cent to 183 million. The number of rounds of 100,000 dollars or more dropped by 22 per cent and active investors by 16 per cent, while volatile currencies and few exits continue to deter Europeans. The FinTech 2.0 bet will only pay off if the portfolio can raise Series A money from a shrinking pool of investors.

meldungen.titel: City Layers: the Vienna start-up behind the "Suderplan" complaints map wants to sell civic participation
meldungen.text:
More than 4,900 complaints and 16,800 reactions in four weeks: the "Wiener Suderplan", an interactive map on which Viennese residents vent about blocked cycle lanes, missing benches and other urban irritations, has become a minor hit. Behind it is City Layers, founded by four people who are not from Vienna at all: Lovro Končar-Gamulin and Domagoj Krhen from Croatia, Androniki Pappa and Angelos Chronis from Greece. That, says Končar-Gamulin, is precisely why the city's famous grumpiness struck them.

The idea grew out of his doctorate at TU Wien and has been developed with research funding since 2023. City Layers builds so-called community maps on which people pin experiences and ideas to specific places; the input is then analysed spatially for urban planning, mobility projects or research. According to the team, the approach has been used in more than ten projects in four countries, reaching over 10,000 people, and in 2025 it was named among the 15 leading science engagement projects at the Falling Walls Science Summit. The Suderplan, which simply asks "what annoys you here?", is meant as a demonstration rather than a rival to the city's own reporting app, Sag's Wien.

The business model is paid campaigns for planning offices, organisations and public bodies: City Layers designs the map, runs the participation, analyses the data and writes the report. Two paid pilots are done, one in the Croatian city of Varaždin, and reusable templates should make each project cheaper to deliver. Funding so far comes mainly from grants (FWF, two EU projects, aws and the Wirtschaftsagentur Wien); the company is only due to be formally incorporated in early 2027. A map of Vienna's Christmas markets is planned before Christmas.

meldungen.titel: From carpenter in the Innviertel to 70 million dollars in New York: Sarah Buchner on AI, speed and Europe's regulatory handicap
meldungen.text:
Sarah Buchner, who grew up in Eitzing in the Innviertel, has one of the more improbable CVs in Austrian tech: trained carpenter, site manager, executive at the construction group Strabag, five completed degrees including an MBA from Stanford. In 2021 she founded Trunk Tools in New York, a construction-tech scale-up that has since raised around 70 million dollars, most recently a 40 million dollar Series B in summer 2025. On a visit to Vienna for the brutkasten MOMENTUM conference, she told brutkasten how the company has changed since.

The money went largely into hiring; Trunk Tools now has about 100 staff. But Buchner says the yardstick has flipped: a year ago start-ups were judged by headcount, today almost the opposite, because so many tasks are handled by AI agents. Right after the Series B, the company began "quite aggressively" building its own agents to run its back office, and its product surface is now roughly 50 times larger than a year ago. Internally she set blunt targets: anyone who had not built their own automated workflow within a week had no future at the firm. "Whoever automates away their own job, we keep," she says, calling it reverse psychology that works. The harder part of AI, she tells customers, is not the technology, which can be tested, but changing how hundreds or thousands of people work.

On politics, she believes that in America business rather than government sets the course, and that AI is pushed above all as a matter of national security, particularly against China. Her view of Europe is sobering: a start-up with global ambitions begins "behind the starting line". In Austria, she says, founders spend six to twelve months asking whether they are even allowed to build a given AI, how, and where the data must sit, whereas in the US the sequence is try, discuss, scale and perhaps regulate at the end.

meldungen.titel: Last call for 2021: the Austrian tax refund for that year must be claimed by 31 December
meldungen.text:
Anyone in Austria who had wage income in 2021 and has not yet filed an employee tax assessment (Arbeitnehmerveranlagung) for that year has until 31 December 2026 to do so. The deadline follows the five-year rule: an assessment can be requested until the end of the fifth year after the tax year in question, so 2021 lapses at the end of this year, while 2025 remains open until 2030. The finance ministry's calendar and KPMG Austria both confirm the date, which also applies to applications for the repayment of wrongly withheld wage tax.

According to KPMG, the assessment can still capture income-related expenses (Werbungskosten), special expenses and extraordinary burdens that were not taken into account during the year, which is where refunds of several hundred euros typically come from, as tabloid oe24 points out. Filing is done online via FinanzOnline. Those who do nothing may still receive an automatic assessment if the conditions are met, but that only happens when the Finanzamt expects a refund on the basis of the data it already holds, and it will not include expenses it does not know about.
